title: Pakistan Consider Pink-Ball Tests After Weather Disrupts Sri Lanka Clash
author: Azmat Nawaz
tags: Pakistan Cricket, Pakistan vs Sri Lanka, Babar Azam, ICC, Mike Hesson, Pink-Ball Test
summary: Mike Hesson and Babar Azam support considering pink-ball Tests in Pakistan after nearly 141 overs were lost against Sri Lanka in Rawalpindi.
body:
![](/images/news/wp/ICC-Cricket-Umpire-Tossing-Ball-1024x683.jpg)

**Mike Hesson and Babar Azam believe pink-ball cricket could help Pakistan avoid losing valuable playing time during its home Test season.**

**RAWALPINDI:** Pakistan could turn to pink-ball cricket for future home Tests after poor light and rain severely disrupted the opening match against Sri Lanka, prompting head coach Mike Hesson and captain Babar Azam to call for a fresh look at how Tests are played during the winter months.

The first Test at Rawalpindi ended in a draw on Friday, with nearly 141 overs lost to weather and fading daylight. Only three innings were possible across five days, leaving both teams with little opportunity to force a result.

Hesson believes the newly approved option of using pink balls in daytime Tests deserves serious consideration, particularly when matches are scheduled during Pakistan's shorter winter days.

"It is certainly something that needs to be talked about for the future series," Hesson told the host broadcaster after the match.

The Pakistan coach pointed out that poor light is likely to remain a problem at this time of year, regardless of which venue hosts the matches.

With the International Cricket Council (ICC) now allowing pink balls to be used in daytime Tests to reduce interruptions, Hesson believes cricket authorities have an opportunity to rethink their approach.

## Babar Azam Welcomes Change but Stresses Preparation

Pakistan captain Babar Azam also welcomed the possibility of using pink balls, although he cautioned against introducing the change without giving players sufficient time to adjust.

Unlike traditional red balls, pink balls behave differently under varying light conditions, making preparation an important part of the transition.

Babar said switching formats at short notice would be difficult, particularly with only a few days separating the two Tests against Sri Lanka.

"A couple of days are not enough to prepare to play a Test with the pink ball," he said during the post-match presentation.

While supporting the idea as a future option, Babar made it clear that teams would need a proper preparation period before making the switch.

![](/images/news/wp/Cricket-Officials-and-a-Red-Ball-1024x576.jpg)

## Nearly 141 Overs Lost in Rawalpindi

The weather played a major role throughout the opening Test, with fading daylight repeatedly forcing the players off the field before the scheduled close.

Rain further complicated matters on the fourth day, when play was abandoned during the afternoon.

Even when the rain stayed away, visibility remained a concern. The umpires were forced to intervene as conditions deteriorated, making it increasingly difficult for batters to safely face the red ball.

Pakistan had attempted to address the issue by scheduling play to begin at 9:30 a.m., earlier than the usual starting time for domestic first-class matches.

However, early morning moisture and dew made an even earlier start impractical.

The match eventually ended in a draw after Pakistan batted through most of the final day, with Saud Shakeel falling short of a century for the second time in the match.

Play was called off at 4:18 p.m., almost two hours before the scheduled finish.

## Winter Weather Creates Scheduling Problems

Hosting Test cricket during November, December and January has become increasingly challenging in parts of Pakistan.

Rawalpindi experiences early sunsets during winter, while Lahore and Multan frequently struggle with smog, fog and poor visibility.

These conditions have already forced the Pakistan Cricket Board (PCB) to change venues for international matches.

The second Test against Sri Lanka, originally scheduled for Lahore, was moved to Rawalpindi because of hazardous smog levels.

Pakistan has faced similar disruptions in previous years, including the relocation of matches involving Zimbabwe and New Zealand.

Karachi generally offers more favorable winter playing conditions, but ongoing renovation work at the National Stadium has limited its availability.

The situation leaves Pakistan with difficult decisions when scheduling home Tests during the colder months.

## Could Pink-Ball Cricket Be the Solution?

![](/images/news/wp/Six-Glossy-Dukes-Cricket-Balls-in-Box-1024x768.jpg)

The ICC's decision to permit pink balls in daytime Tests offers Pakistan a potential way to reduce the number of overs lost to poor light.

Unlike the traditional red ball, the pink ball is designed to remain more visible under artificial lighting, allowing matches to continue when natural daylight begins to fade.

However, introducing it would require careful planning, particularly because players are more accustomed to the red ball in conventional Test cricket.

For now, Pakistan and Sri Lanka will continue with the red ball in the second Test, with neither board pursuing a late switch.

But after another weather-affected contest in Rawalpindi, the discussion surrounding pink-ball Tests is likely to continue.

For Hesson and Babar, the priority is clear: finding a practical way to ensure more cricket is played and fewer Test matches are decided by the weather rather than performances on the field.

title: David Warner Accuses Cricket Australia of Cover-Up in 2018 Sandpapergate Investigation
author: Tariq Mureed
tags: David Warner, Pat Cummins, Australia Cricket, Usman Khawaja, Sandpapergate, Cricket Australia, Ball Tampering
summary: David Warner allegations raise fresh questions about Cricket Australia's 2018 investigation and the claims involving Pat Cummins.
body:
![](/images/news/wp/Australian-Cricketer-at-Press-Conference-1-1024x683.jpg)

**Former Australia opener David Warner has questioned Cricket Australia's handling of the 2018 ball-tampering scandal, alleging that key bowlers were never interviewed during the original investigation.**

The controversy surrounding Australia's 2018 ball-tampering scandal has taken another dramatic turn, with former opener David Warner accusing Cricket Australia (CA) of conducting a flawed investigation and questioning whether the full story was ever uncovered.

Warner's latest comments come amid growing tensions between several members of Australia's 2018 Test squad, following allegations made by Usman Khawaja in his recently published book.

In an Instagram post on Saturday, Warner questioned why fast bowlers Josh Hazlewood and Mitchell Starc, along with spinner Nathan Lyon, were reportedly not interviewed during Cricket Australia's original investigation into the Newlands scandal.

"As far as I am aware, CA did not interview Josh Hazlewood, Mitchell Starc or Nathan Lyon in their 2018 investigation," Warner wrote.

He argued that if those players were not questioned, Cricket Australia could not confidently maintain that the bowling group had no knowledge of the ball-tampering plan.

Warner went further, suggesting the investigation had been designed to place responsibility on certain individuals rather than establish everything that happened.

"That stinks of a cover up," he wrote.

His accusations have brought fresh attention to one of Australian cricket's most damaging controversies, nearly eight years after the incident in South Africa.

## Cricket Australia Responds to Warner's Allegations

Cricket Australia rejected the suggestion that players had been denied an opportunity to provide information during the original investigation.

A CA spokesperson said everyone involved had been given the chance to speak when the matter was first examined and could have submitted additional evidence at any point over the following eight years.

However, the governing body's response did not directly confirm whether Hazlewood, Starc and Lyon had been formally interviewed.

Cricket Australia chief executive Todd Greenberg has also indicated that there is no sufficient reason to reopen the investigation.

According to Australia captain Pat Cummins, Greenberg reviewed the original records after learning about Khawaja's forthcoming book and found nothing that justified another inquiry.

Despite the renewed allegations, Cricket Australia has not announced any plans to revisit the case.

![](/images/news/wp/Cricket-Press-Conference-Microphone-Array-1024x683.jpg)

## Pat Cummins Rejects Khawaja's Claims

The dispute intensified on Friday when Cummins addressed the allegations during a lengthy press conference in Sydney.

Cummins strongly denied knowing that sandpaper would be taken onto the field during the 2018 South Africa tour.

He also rejected suggestions that he or other members of the bowling group had helped plan the ball-tampering operation.

"If by that he means that we knew sandpaper was going out on the field, he's 100 percent wrong," Cummins said.

The Australian captain described the allegation that he helped devise the scheme as "complete and utter nonsense."

Cummins also expressed disappointment with Khawaja, saying he had been shocked by claims in the book that Khawaja warned Cameron Bancroft to be careful when using sandpaper.

Although Cummins acknowledged his friendship with Khawaja, he said the allegations had serious implications for the reputations of players and Australian cricket.

He maintained that he had consistently denied knowledge of the sandpaper plan since the scandal first emerged.

## Warner Stands Firmly Behind Khawaja

Warner has made it clear that he supports Khawaja's account of events.

Speaking during coverage of Australia's first ODI against England in Perth on Friday, the former opener criticized Cummins' handling of the controversy.

Warner said he continued to believe Khawaja's version of events and was disappointed by the Australian captain's public response.

"I still stick by Uzzy and what he's written in that book. It's the truth, and I really support him," Warner said.

He also accused Cummins of throwing Khawaja "under the bus" during the press conference.

The disagreement has exposed a significant divide between former teammates who were part of Australia's Test setup during the 2018 tour.

![](/images/news/wp/Laughing-Australian-Cricket-Press-Panel-1024x683.jpg)

## Fresh Questions Over the South Africa Tour

Khawaja's book has also raised questions about events during the second Test in Port Elizabeth, now known as Gqeberha.

According to his account, Bancroft used sandpaper on the ball after retrieving it near the boundary, where it had been left by the umpires.

Cummins said the account was new to him and that he had never been aware of such an incident.

He explained that the practice of leaving the ball near the boundary was no longer part of Test cricket, with umpires now handing it directly to players in the middle.

Meanwhile, Starc has maintained his support for a joint statement issued by Australia's frontline bowlers in 2021, in which they denied knowing that foreign objects were being taken onto the field at Newlands.

The conflicting accounts have renewed debate about what individual players knew during the controversial tour.

## Marnus Labuschagne Concerned by Growing Dispute

Australia batter Marnus Labuschagne, who was not part of the 2018 South Africa squad, has expressed concern about the public disagreement.

Speaking after Queensland's Sheffield Shield victory over Tasmania, Labuschagne said the situation was difficult to watch.

He acknowledged that Khawaja had shared his account through his book and Cummins had responded publicly, but stressed that he could not comment on events he had not witnessed.

Labuschagne said he doubted anyone was enjoying the controversy surrounding Australian cricket.

## Will the Investigation Be Reopened?

For now, Cricket Australia remains unwilling to launch another investigation, despite Warner's latest accusations.

Khawaja's scheduled book-signing appearance in Merrylands was postponed, while a planned interview with the Grade Cricketer podcast was moved to Thursday.

Cameron Bancroft is reportedly still considering whether to speak publicly, while Steven Smith is expected to return to Australia from New York next week.

Their potential comments could bring further attention to the controversy.

Eight years after the sandpaper scandal damaged Australian cricket's reputation, questions about the events in South Africa continue to divide former teammates.

With Warner challenging the investigation and Cummins firmly rejecting Khawaja's allegations, the dispute appears far from settled.
seoTitle: David Warner Accuses Cricket Australia of Cover-Up
seoDescription: David Warner allegations raise fresh questions about Cricket Australia's 2018 investigation and the claims involving Pat Cummins.

title: Jay Shah Re-Elected ICC Chair as New Cricket Calendar Opens Door for IPL Expansion
author: Tariq Mureed
tags: BCCI, ICC, International Cricket, Jay Shah, IPL 2028, IPL Expansion
summary: Jay Shah is re-elected ICC chair as a revised cricket calendar opens the door for a possible 12-team IPL expansion in 2028.
body:
**The ICC's revised tournament schedule could give the Indian Premier League more room to grow, with a 12-team competition reportedly under consideration for 2028.**

Jay Shah will continue leading the International Cricket Council (ICC) after securing another term as chairman without opposition, following a board meeting in Bali that also brought significant changes to international cricket's future calendar.

While Shah's re-election was a major development, the ICC's decision to reshape its men's tournament schedule could have an even greater impact on the game.

Under the revised calendar, major ICC men's events between 2028 and 2035 will largely take place outside the March-to-May period, potentially giving the Indian Premier League (IPL) a longer and more predictable window.

The move comes as discussions continue over expanding the IPL from its current 10 teams to 12, potentially beginning in 2028.

## ICC Calendar Creates More Space for the IPL

The new scheduling arrangement marks a shift from recent years, when major international competitions such as the T20 World Cup and Champions Trophy occupied parts of February and March.

Most ICC men's tournaments from 2028 onward are now scheduled for the second half of the calendar year, leaving March, April and May largely free of global events.

Although the Future Tours Programme for bilateral international cricket has not yet been finalized, people familiar with those discussions have indicated that major international series are also unlikely to be scheduled during that period.

If those arrangements are confirmed, the IPL could benefit from a more consistent annual window, reducing potential scheduling conflicts and improving player availability.

## IPL Could Expand to 12 Teams in 2028

![](/images/news/wp/Stadium-trophy-with-purple-ribbons-1024x683.jpg)

The possibility of a larger IPL has gained attention following reports in India that Pune and Vadodara were being considered as locations for two additional franchises.

The Board of Control for Cricket in India (BCCI) has dismissed those reports, and no formal decision on expansion has been announced.

However, the league is reportedly examining ways to grow beyond its existing 10-team format.

One possibility would see the competition increase to 12 franchises, with each team facing every other side twice during the league stage.

Such an arrangement could increase the number of matches from 74 to 94, creating additional broadcasting opportunities and a significantly longer competition.

Any expansion would need to account for player workloads, international commitments and the availability of suitable venues.

## Broadcasting Revenue Remains a Major Factor

The IPL's commercial success has been driven in large part by its enormous broadcasting audience and valuable media rights agreements.

Its current domestic media rights arrangement is valued at approximately $6 billion over five years.

Following the merger of Disney's Indian media operations with Reliance Industries' media interests in 2024, the creation of JioStar has changed the country's broadcasting landscape.

With the next IPL media rights cycle approaching, increasing the number of matches could provide the league with additional commercial opportunities.

More fixtures would mean additional advertising inventory and broadcasting content, although a larger tournament would not automatically guarantee higher rights valuations.

## World Test Championship Finals Retain June Window

The ICC's calendar changes will not affect every major event in the same way.

The 2034 men's T20 World Cup is scheduled for June and July, while World Test Championship finals are set to continue taking place in June during odd-numbered years through 2035.

England is expected to remain a leading candidate to stage those finals.

The England and Wales Cricket Board already has an agreement to host World Test Championship finals through 2031, with a possible extension covering subsequent editions.

## Jay Shah to Remain ICC Chairman Until 2030

Shah's unopposed re-election provides continuity at the ICC during a period when international cricket is facing important decisions over scheduling, franchise leagues and commercial growth.

The former BCCI secretary is now expected to remain in office until December 2030, when the ICC's constitutional term limits will require him to step down.

Following his re-election, Shah described the position as both an honor and a responsibility, emphasizing the importance of cooperation among cricket's member nations.

He also reaffirmed his commitment to developing the sport internationally and ensuring that decisions taken during his leadership deliver long-term benefits.

## What the Changes Mean for International Cricket

The revised calendar could represent an important shift in the relationship between international cricket and domestic franchise competitions.

A protected IPL window would provide greater scheduling certainty for franchises, broadcasters and players. At the same time, national cricket boards would need to organize bilateral series around an increasingly crowded global calendar.

For the IPL, the changes create an opportunity to consider a larger competition without directly clashing with major ICC tournaments.

For international cricket, the challenge will be maintaining a balance between the commercial strength of franchise leagues and the importance of national-team competitions.

With the new ICC calendar taking shape and IPL expansion still under discussion, the next few years could bring substantial changes to how the global cricket season is organized.

title: Usman Khawaja Reveals Family Has Faced Backlash Over Sandpapergate Claims
author: News Desk

summary: Usman Khawaja reveals how his wife and family have been affected by the backlash over his Sandpapergate claims
body:
![](/images/news/wp/ChatGPT-Image-Nov-16-2026-07_19_49-PM.jpg)

**Former Australia opener Usman Khawaja says the reaction to his new book has become deeply personal, with his wife and family caught up in the controversy surrounding the 2018 ball-tampering scandal.**

Usman Khawaja expected his new book to spark difficult conversations about Australian cricket's past. What he did not anticipate was how deeply the reaction would affect the people closest to him.

The former Australian Test opener has revealed that his family, including his wife Rachel, has been caught up in the backlash following the release of his memoir, *Sabr*, which has reignited debate over the 2018 ball-tampering scandal.

Speaking on the *They Used to Be* podcast, Khawaja acknowledged that revisiting one of Australian cricket's most controversial episodes was always going to attract criticism. However, he admitted that some of the response had crossed into territory he had not expected.

"There has been a cost to my family too," Khawaja said.

The former batter explained that while he was prepared to face criticism himself, the personal nature of the reaction had been difficult to accept.

"I just didn't realise it would be so personal," he added.

## Khawaja's Book Reopens the Sandpapergate Debate

The controversy began after Khawaja suggested in his memoir that responsibility for the 2018 Cape Town ball-tampering incident extended beyond the three players who were formally sanctioned.

David Warner, Steve Smith and Cameron Bancroft received punishments following the scandal, which damaged Australian cricket's reputation and prompted major changes within the national team.

Khawaja's suggestion that the incident involved a wider collective responsibility has drawn strong responses from former teammates.

Australia captain Pat Cummins and fast bowler Mitchell Starc have rejected the implication that other members of the side knew about the plan.

The disagreement has brought renewed attention to an incident that many within Australian cricket had hoped was firmly in the past.

![](/images/news/wp/Family-Memories-at-the-Cricket-Ground-3.jpg)

## Khawaja Says He Wanted to Defend His Former Teammates

Khawaja explained that his intention was not to create another division within Australian cricket.

Instead, he wanted to express support for players he believes were treated unfairly while being mindful of those still representing the national team.

"I have stood up for three guys I feel like were treated unfairly," Khawaja told podcast host Antoinette Lattouf.

He acknowledged that speaking publicly about the scandal could have consequences for current players and said he had tried to approach the subject carefully.

For Khawaja, the challenge has been finding a way to defend his friends without placing unnecessary pressure on others.

He also made it clear that he was not seeking sympathy over the reaction to his comments. He understood that publishing his account of the scandal would invite scrutiny, even if he underestimated how personal the criticism might become.

![](/images/news/wp/ChatGPT-Image-Nov-16-2026-07_19_55-PM-2.jpg)

## Warner Friendship Remains Strong Despite Controversy

Away from the dispute, Khawaja has continued to speak warmly about his longstanding friendship with David Warner.

Appearing on Channel 10's *Sam Pang Tonight* on Monday, the former opener discussed his relationship with Warner, his family life and the story of how he proposed to Rachel.

The program did not address the renewed Sandpapergate controversy or the public disagreement involving Cummins.

When asked about Warner, Khawaja described their friendship as a connection between two very different personalities.

"Me and Davey are very different people," he said.

Despite those differences, Khawaja explained that they share similar values when it comes to family, loyalty and looking after the people around them.

He suggested that Warner's public image does not always reflect the qualities that have helped sustain their friendship over the years.

## More Public Appearances Ahead for Khawaja

Khawaja is expected to continue discussing his life and cricket career during an appearance on *The Grade Cricketer* podcast on Thursday.

He is also scheduled to participate in the Gold Clash celebrity cricket match in Cairns on Sunday, where he could cross paths with former Australia coach Darren Lehmann.

Lehmann was in charge of the national team when the ball-tampering scandal unfolded in South Africa in 2018. He has consistently maintained that he had no prior knowledge of the plan.

Whether the latest controversy leads to further public exchanges remains uncertain.

For now, Khawaja's comments have added a personal dimension to a debate that has largely centered on accountability, team culture and what really happened in Cape Town eight years ago.

His account has reopened difficult questions about Australian cricket's past, but the former opener's latest concern is the impact those discussions are having on his family.

Imran Khan, the captain who led Pakistan to their first men’s Cricket World Cup title in 1992, has asked the country’s top judges to secure urgent medical care for him and his wife, Bushra Bibi. In a letter made public on November 16, the former prime minister warned that he “may not return alive” if his confinement continues under present conditions.

Khan made the appeal through his lawyer, Salman Safdar, who spent three hours with him at Adiala Jail in Rawalpindi on November 11. Safdar said Khan gave him notes and asked him to take his concerns to the chief justices of Pakistan’s Supreme Court, Federal Constitutional Court and Islamabad High Court.

## Khan says he is still waiting for a hospital examination

The 74-year-old said he had lost 85 per cent of the sight in his right eye. He also said doctors had warned him that he was at risk of a brain haemorrhage or cardiac arrest. His request to the judges was to enforce an order the Supreme Court had issued nearly three months earlier.

On August 18, the court directed authorities to take Khan to Shifa International Hospital in Islamabad for an independent examination. Khan said that visit had yet to take place. He received an eye injection at the state-run Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences on November 10. The hospital described him as “clinically stable” after the visit, and Parliamentary Affairs Minister Tariq Fazal Chaudhry said he was receiving the care he needed.

Khan also expressed concern for his wife’s eyesight. He said Bushra Bibi had surgery for a detached retina in April and could lose her sight permanently without a second operation. On November 16, her lawyers asked the Islamabad High Court for her medical records and an immediate transfer to a specialist hospital.

## Former cricket captains wrote to Pakistan’s prime minister

![](/images/news/wp/Imran-Khan-with-Pakistan-teammates.jpg)

Months before Khan made his plea to the judges, some of his former opponents had raised the issue with Pakistan’s government. In February, 14 former international captains wrote to Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif after reports that Khan’s eyesight had deteriorated in prison. India’s Sunil Gavaskar and Kapil Dev were among those who asked the government to ensure he received proper medical care.

A second letter followed in August, after the Supreme Court ordered the hospital examination. This time, 21 former captains urged Sharif’s government to carry out the order. The signatories included Australia’s Allan Border and Steve Waugh, England’s Nasser Hussain and the West Indies’ Clive Lloyd.

Khan’s defining moment as Pakistan captain came in the 1992 World Cup final against England in Melbourne. He top-scored for Pakistan with 72, then took the final wicket himself to seal a 22-run win and the country’s first men’s World Cup title.

title: Pakistan bowl Sri Lanka out for 98 to take control of second Test
author: Azmat Nawaz
tags: Pakistan Cricket, Sri Lanka Cricket, Pakistan vs Sri Lanka, Mohammad Abbas, Aamer Jamal, Razaullah, Azan Awais
summary: Pakistan bowled Sri Lanka out for 98 before reaching 121-3 on day one of the second Test in Rawalpindi, with Azan Awais unbeaten on 47.
body:
![](/images/news/wp/Three-cricketers-in-a-stadium-portrait-1024x683.jpg)

**Rawalpindi: **Pakistan’s fast bowlers put the hosts in charge of the second Test in Rawalpindi on Tuesday, dismissing Sri Lanka for 98 before reaching stumps on 121-3, a lead of 23 runs.

Mohammad Abbas, Razaullah and Aamer Jamal shared nine wickets as Pakistan made full use of a green-tinged pitch after choosing to bowl. Sri Lanka lasted just 35.3 overs, with only Kusal Mendis and Sonal Dinusha offering sustained resistance.

Azan Awais then helped Pakistan build on that advantage, finishing unbeaten on 47 alongside nightwatchman Saqib Khan on two.

## Pakistan’s pace attack leaves Sri Lanka struggling

Saqib, fresh from taking seven wickets on debut in the drawn first Test, struck in the fourth over. He removed Pasindu Sooriyabandara for two, with wicketkeeper Ghazi Ghori taking the catch.

Abbas followed with two important wickets. Dinesh Chandimal was caught at short leg for seven before Kamindu Mendis fell for eight, leaving Sri Lanka 25-3.

Razaullah kept the pressure on, dismissing Lahiru Udara for four after a difficult 34-ball stay and trapping first-Test centurion Dhananjaya de Silva lbw for one. At 36-5, Sri Lanka were already facing a fight to put together a competitive total.

## Jamal ends Sri Lanka’s brief recovery

![](/images/news/wp/Three-Pakistani-cricketers-in-the-stadium-1024x683.jpg)

Kusal Mendis and Sonal Dinusha steadied the innings with a 49-run sixth-wicket stand, giving Sri Lanka some relief after the early damage.

Kusal made 32 from 50 balls, hitting five boundaries, while Dinusha scored 21 off 40 deliveries with four fours.

Jamal ended their resistance with the short ball. Kusal mistimed a hook before Dinusha also fell trying to pull, opening the way for Pakistan to finish off the innings.

Sri Lanka lost their final four wickets for 13 runs. Razaullah bowled Milan Rathnayake for a duck, Abbas held a return catch to remove Prabath Jayasuriya for three, and Jamal dismissed Lahiru Kumara to complete the collapse.

Abbas led the attack with 3-14, supported by Razaullah’s 3-21 and Jamal’s 3-24. Saqib took the remaining wicket.

## Azan Awais keeps Pakistan ahead at stumps

![](/images/news/wp/ChatGPT-Image-Nov-17-2026-12_47_32-PM-1024x640.jpg)

Pakistan’s reply began with an 80-run opening partnership between Tayyab Arif and Awais, putting the hosts within reach of Sri Lanka’s total.

Tayyab scored 46 before the visitors claimed three wickets in the final session to regain some ground.

Awais, however, remained composed and finished three runs short of a half-century. With seven wickets in hand and a first-innings lead already secured, Pakistan will begin day two with a chance to stretch their advantage.

title: Cameron Bancroft says Cummins left him feeling ‘betrayed’, claims whole team knew about Sandpapergate
author: Tariq Mureed
tags: Pat Cummins, Sandpapergate, Cricket Australia, Australian Cricket, Cameron Bancroft, Ball-tampering
summary: Cameron Bancroft claims Australia's whole team knew about Sandpapergate, challenges Pat Cummins' denial and admits withholding details from investigators.
body:
![](/images/news/wp/Australian-Cricketer-at-Press-Conference-2-1024x683.jpg)

Cameron Bancroft has accused the Australian team of knowing about the use of sandpaper during the 2018 tour of South Africa, saying recent comments from Pat Cummins left him feeling “angry, betrayed and alone”.

Writing in The West Australian, Bancroft alleged that knowledge of the ball-tampering extended beyond the three players Cricket Australia punished: himself, Steve Smith and David Warner.

His account directly challenges previous denials from Australia’s bowlers and raises fresh questions about how the scandal was handled.

### Bancroft says sandpaper use began before Cape Town

Bancroft claimed the practice began during the second Test in Port Elizabeth, before television cameras caught him tampering with the ball at Newlands in Cape Town.

According to his account, the plan was discussed during a team meeting at tea on the second day. He alleged that head coach Darren Lehmann and bowling coach David Saker were present, while Smith distanced himself from the proposal.

Bancroft acknowledged that he knew the tactic was cheating. However, he said his desire to contribute as a young player finding his place in the Test side influenced his decision to take part.

He alleged that bowlers gave him feedback during play about whether his work on the ball was producing reverse swing. He also claimed teammates discussed the practice openly and that his contribution was praised after Australia took four wickets late in the day.

These allegations remain disputed. Australia’s leading bowlers have previously denied knowing about the plan to use sandpaper at Newlands.

### Bancroft admits withholding details from investigators

Bancroft also acknowledged that he did not give Cricket Australia’s original investigation a full account of what happened.

He said he withheld information about when the practice started, how long it continued and who knew about it because he did not want to implicate others.

That admission is central to his latest account, which describes wider involvement than the version established publicly after the scandal.

Bancroft said the same approach continued in Cape Town, where cameras filmed him rubbing sandpaper against the ball before attempting to hide it.

The incident led to bans for Bancroft, Smith and Warner and became one of the most damaging episodes in Australian cricket.

### Why Cummins’ comments prompted Bancroft to speak

![](/images/news/wp/Australian-Cricketer-at-Press-Conference-1-1-1024x683.jpg)

Bancroft said Usman Khawaja’s recent account of the controversy encouraged him to share his own experience. But it was Cummins’ press conference last week that prompted him to respond publicly.

The Australia captain denied knowing that sandpaper had been used. Bancroft said hearing that denial brought back painful memories of the tour and its aftermath.

He also described his distress at the joint statement issued by Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon in 2021, which denied knowledge of the plan to bring sandpaper onto the field at Newlands.

Bancroft alleged that conversations and feedback he remembered from the field were difficult to reconcile with those public statements.

He further claimed that a team meeting after the Cape Town Test focused on limiting the fallout, rather than teammates expressing surprise about what had happened. He said he felt he had been left to carry responsibility for conduct others knew about.

### Cricket Australia establishes independent forum

![](/images/news/wp/Cricket-Press-Conference-Microphone-Array-1-1024x683.jpg)

Cricket Australia announced an independent forum for players and staff involved in the 2018 tour to share their recollections. Bancroft intends to participate.

Responding to his article, the governing body said it would consider his comments and was finalising the forum’s terms of reference before beginning the process.

The forum comes amid renewed debate sparked by Khawaja’s autobiography and subsequent comments from other members of the touring group.

### Lehmann and Cummins’ representatives respond

Lehmann, who has previously denied knowing about the use of sandpaper, told ABC he needed time to consider the allegations before providing a detailed response.

Cummins’ management said the issues raised in Bancroft’s account had already been addressed by the captain at his recent press conference.

With Bancroft’s allegations conflicting with those earlier denials, the accounts of what happened in South Africa remain sharply divided. The independent forum will give those involved an opportunity to put their recollections on record.
seoTitle: Bancroft claims whole team knew about Sandpapergate
seoDescription: Cameron Bancroft claims Australia's whole team knew about Sandpapergate, challenges Pat Cummins' denial and admits withholding details from investigators.
